theme: Stages of the journey; boundaries of the land
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 33:1-34:29. The first chapter is a travel diary of the entire journey from Egypt. The second sets out the boundaries of the land. Read the first as a testimony to God’s faithfulness, and the second as a promise coming close.
settingTheScene: Israel is about to cross the Jordan. Before they do, Moses records every stage of the journey from Egypt to the plains of Moab. There are forty-two stops. The record is written “by command of the LORD.” Then God defines the borders of the land, names the leaders who will divide it, and gives instructions for the conquest.
observation: “Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD” (33:2).
The list begins with Rameses and ends with the plains of Moab by the Jordan (33:3-49).
Some of the stops are well known: the sea, Marah, Elim, Rephidim, Sinai, Kibroth-hattaavah, Kadesh (33:8-37).
Aaron died on Mount Hor at the age of 123 (33:38-39).
“When you pass over the Jordan into the land of Canaan, then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you” (33:51-52).
Failure to drive them out will make them “as barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides” (33:55).
The borders of the land are described on the south, west, north, and east (34:1-12).
Eleazar and Joshua, with one leader from each tribe, will divide the land (34:16-29).
interpretation:
A list of travel stops is not what we would choose to read for inspiration, but it says something important. Forty-two stages. Each name is a place where God’s people camped, and where something happened. Some were places of failure, some of provision, and some of grief. The list shows that the whole journey, even the part that felt like wasted time, was part of God’s plan. “By command of the LORD,” Moses wrote it down.

The record is also a way of remembering. In the Psalms, the people are repeatedly told to recall the journey. This list gives a map for memory. If we want to understand God’s faithfulness, we need to look back over the stages of our own lives and see how he led us. Few of us remember every stage. But God does.

The shift to the land of Canaan marks the end of the wilderness. For the first time since leaving Egypt, the people are given a goal with edges. The borders are described in detail, because the land is a gift with specific limits. It is real, and it is theirs.

The warning in 33:55 is sobering. If they do not drive out the inhabitants, those left will become “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides.” The danger was not military but spiritual. Peoples who worshiped other gods would be a constant temptation. The book of Judges will show how it came true.

The assignment of leaders to divide the land is a final note of order. Eleazar the priest and Joshua the leader will work with one chief from each tribe. The land is not seized by individuals but received by the community, under the guidance of God’s chosen leaders.
connection: Hebrews 11:13-16 describes the patriarchs as people who “confessed that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” and who longed for a heavenly country. Paul says that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28), including the wanderings. Peter describes believers as “sojourners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11). The new Jerusalem has boundaries too, and its dimensions are given in Revelation 21:15-17.
application:
Take a few minutes to list the stages of your own journey with God. Where have you seen his faithfulness?

Ask whether there is a “thorn in your side,” something you have left unresolved. Take a step to deal with it.

Thank God that your journey has a destination, and that he is leading you there.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for leading you stage by stage, remembering a step you can name.
Ask him to help you deal with the “thorns” you have left behind.
Look forward with him to the land he has promised.
